title: const references
learningGoals: know when to use const and ampersand

youtube.title: C++ const References: Fast and Safe Parameters | C++ Programming EP 25
youtube.description: In this episode you will pass big values without copying, protect a parameter with const and know when to use const and ampersand, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 const references · 0:49 A const reference · 1:29 Which parameter style? · 1:59 Second program · 2:59 Recap · 3:29 Bug of the Day · 4:17 Challenge · 4:37 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a glass case around a big box

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we learn the most common parameter style in modern C plus plus. It is fast, and it is safe.

scenes.onScreen: "const references": numbered lines (1. A copy of a big value is slow; 2. A reference avoids the copy; 3. Const stops the function from changing it) and an analogy card: a museum: you may look at the painting, but you may not touch it
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Copying a big string for every call is slow. A reference avoids the copy. But a reference lets the function change the original. Add const, and the function may only read it. So a const reference is fast and safe. Think of a museum. You may look at the painting, but you may not touch it.
points: A copy of a big value is slow
Const stops the function from changing it

analogy.title: const references
analogy.body: A museum: you may look at the painting, but you may not touch it

scenes.onScreen: show.cpp: show reads a string without copying it
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The parameter is a const reference to a string. No copy is made. [HL 6] The function may read text, but it may not change it. [HL 11] Main passes the string. [HL 6] The function prints it. Use this style for strings and other big values.

scenes.onScreen: a table of three parameter styles
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Here are three styles. A plain parameter makes a copy and cannot change the original. A reference makes no copy and can change the original. A const reference makes no copy and cannot change the original. For big values that you only read, choose the last style.

diagram.caption: a table of three parameter styles

scenes.onScreen: longer.cpp: longer takes two const references
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Both parameters are const references. Both strings are only read. [HL 6] The function compares the sizes. [HL 12] Panjim and Mapusa both have six letters, so the answer is false. [HL 13] A const reference can also take a plain quoted text. Margao is longer than Goa, so the answer is true.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as longer dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints false and then true.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A copy of a big value is slow. Two. A const reference makes no copy. Three. The function may read the value but not change it. Four. A const reference can take a temporary value. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A copy of a big value is slow.
A const reference makes no copy.
The function may read the value but not change it.
A const reference can take a temporary value.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Changing a const reference
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The function takes a const reference, and then tries to add one. The compiler says increment of read-only reference. Const means look, but do not touch. If the function must change the value, remove const.

scenes.onScreen: The museum guard loves const references. He says, look all you want, but do not touch the exhibit.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: The museum guard loves const references. He says, look all you want, but do not touch the exhibit.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: choose the right parameter style
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that prints the size of a string. Choose the best parameter style, and explain your choice in a comment. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 26 · Default arguments and overloading

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

bump.cpp: In function 'void bump(const int&)':
bump.cpp:5:5: error: increment of read-only reference 'n'
    5 |     n++;
      |     ^
bug.why: A const reference is read-only. If the function must change the value, use a plain reference. If it must not, remove the change.

pun: "The museum guard loves const references. He says, look all you want, but do not touch the exhibit."
challenge: Write a function that prints the size of a string. Choose the best parameter style, and explain your choice in a comment.
challengeAnswer: Use const string ampersand. The function only reads the string, and a reference avoids a slow copy.
